# Fenwick trees without black boxes

A Fenwick tree, also called a binary indexed tree, stores prefix
information in an array `bit[1..n]`. The key idea is that index `i`
owns a block whose length is the value of its lowest set bit:

```text
lowbit(i) = i & -i

bit[i] stores the sum of:
i-lowbit(i)+1, ..., i
```

## Why choose exactly these blocks?

Start from the operation we want: `prefix(r)` must add all values from `1` to
`r`, while a point update must avoid rewriting every later prefix. Storing all
prefix sums makes queries instant but updates linear. Storing only individual
values makes updates instant but queries linear. A Fenwick tree keeps a small
set of reusable, power-of-two blocks between those two extremes.

Imagine building those blocks in layers:

```text
Every index owns its final 1 element.
Every multiple of 2 can summarize its final 2 elements.
Every multiple of 4 can summarize its final 4 elements.
Every multiple of 8 can summarize its final 8 elements.
...
```

At index `i`, keep the largest block from this list that ends at `i`. Thus:

```text
odd i                       owns 1 element
i divisible by 2, not 4     owns 2 elements
i divisible by 4, not 8     owns 4 elements
i divisible by 8, not 16    owns 8 elements
```

The largest power of two dividing `i` is exactly `lowbit(i)`. In binary, it is
the value represented by the rightmost `1` bit:

```text
i       binary      lowbit     block ending at i
3       0011        1          [3,3]
4       0100        4          [1,4]
6       0110        2          [5,6]
8       1000        8          [1,8]
```

This alignment is what makes the blocks fit together. To answer `prefix(r)`,
take the largest stored block ending at `r`. The still-missing part ends just
before that block, at `r - lowbit(r)`, so repeat there. Each subtraction clears
the rightmost `1` bit of `r`. For `r = 13`, whose binary form is `1101`, the
block sizes are `1`, then `4`, then `8`; they cover the prefix without gaps or
overlap.

A point update walks the same hierarchy in reverse. If position `i` changes,
update the block ending at `i`, then the next larger aligned block containing
that position. The move `i += lowbit(i)` performs the necessary binary carry
to reach its next owner. For position `3`, that gives `3 -> 4 -> 8`.

So the Fenwick layout is not an arbitrary trick: it is a compact hierarchy of
aligned power-of-two suffixes. Binary representation tells us both how to
decompose a prefix and how to find every stored block affected by an update.

Example for `n = 8`:

```text
i       lowbit(i)    covered segment
1       1            [1,1]
2       2            [1,2]
3       1            [3,3]
4       4            [1,4]
5       1            [5,5]
6       2            [5,6]
7       1            [7,7]
8       8            [1,8]
```

## The picture to keep in mind

For `n = 8`, this is the whole structure. Each horizontal bar is one entry
of `bit`; it owns the highlighted interval, not just the value at its index.
The bars overlap on purpose.

For example, position `3` belongs to exactly the three block owners that an
update visits: `bit[3]`, `bit[4]`, and `bit[8]`. Conversely, `prefix(6)`
reads the two disjoint bars `bit[6]` (`[5,6]`) and `bit[4]` (`[1,4]`), which
together cover `[1,6]` exactly once.

To compute a prefix sum `sum(i)`, repeatedly take the block ending
at `i`, then jump to the index just before that block:

```text
answer += bit[i]
i -= i & -i
```

This decomposes `[1,i]` into disjoint power-of-two blocks. For
`i = 13`, the visited indices are:

```text
13 -> 12 -> 8 -> 0
[13,13] + [9,12] + [1,8]
```

To add `delta` to position `i`, every Fenwick block containing `i`
must increase by `delta`. Those block owners are found by moving
upward:

```text
bit[i] += delta
i += i & -i
```

Both loops touch at most one index per binary digit, so each
operation costs `O(log n)`.

## Building intuition with one update

Suppose `n = 8` and we add `+5` at position `3`.

The update visits:

```text
3 -> 4 -> 8
```

Those are exactly the Fenwick blocks that contain position `3`:

```text
bit[3] covers [3,3]
bit[4] covers [1,4]
bit[8] covers [1,8]
```

No other block ending at another index includes position `3`, so no other
Fenwick entry changes.

For `sum(6)`, the query visits:

```text
6 -> 4 -> 0
```

and reads:

```text
bit[6] covers [5,6]
bit[4] covers [1,4]
```

Together these blocks form `[1,6]` without overlap.

# Coordinate compression with Fenwick

## The problem: values are not usable indices

A Fenwick tree is an array, so its indices must be small positive integers.
But values in a problem may be negative, sparse, or as large as `10^9`:

```text
a = [50, -10, 50, 900]
```

We cannot access `bit[-10]`, and allocating `bit[1..900]` for only three
different values wastes space. For order-based problems, however, the exact
distances between values do not matter. We only need to know which value is
smaller, equal, or larger.

Coordinate compression creates one dense Fenwick index for each distinct
value.

## Step 1: build the value-to-rank map

Copy the values, sort them, and remove duplicates:

```text
sorted distinct values = [-10, 50, 900]
```

Number that sorted list starting from 1:

```text
value   -10    50    900
rank      1     2      3
```

The rank of a value is therefore one plus the number of distinct values smaller
than it. Equal values look up the same rank.

## Step 2: translate the array

Use the map on each original value:

```text
original value          50   -10   50   900
compressed rank          2     1    2     3
```

Compression preserves order and equality:

```text
x < y  iff  rank(x) < rank(y)
x = y  iff  rank(x) = rank(y)
```

It does not preserve distances: ranks `2` and `3` differ by one even though
`900 - 50 = 850`. That is fine for counting smaller or larger values, but not
for calculations that need the original numeric differences.

## Step 3: decide what the Fenwick tree stores

In inversion counting, scan the array from left to right. The scan still uses
the original array positions. The Fenwick index is different: it is the
value's compressed rank.

Store a frequency at each rank:

```text
add(rank(x), 1) means: one more value x has been seen
prefix(k)       means: how many seen values have rank at most k
```

For `x = 50`, whose rank is `2`:

```text
prefix(1) = number of previous values < 50
prefix(2) = number of previous values <= 50
```

Including rank `2` counts earlier values equal to `50`. Therefore the number of
earlier values strictly greater than the current value is:

```text
number_seen - prefix(rank(current_value))
```

## A short inversion trace

Process `[50, -10, 50, 900]`, whose ranks are `[2,1,2,3]`:

```text
current   seen before    count <= current    count > current
50        []             0                   0
-10       [50]           0                   1
50        [50,-10]       2                   0
900       [50,-10,50]    3                   0
```

The total is one inversion: `(50,-10)`.

## Implementation recipe

C++:

```cpp
vector<long long> values = a;
sort(values.begin(), values.end());
values.erase(unique(values.begin(), values.end()), values.end());

int rank = int(lower_bound(values.begin(), values.end(), x) - values.begin()) + 1;
```

Python:

```python
values = sorted(set(a))
rank = {value: index + 1 for index, value in enumerate(values)}
```

The `+1` is essential because Fenwick trees use 1-based indices.

# Difference arrays and Fenwick

A difference array stores the change when moving one position right. Define
`a[0] = 0`, then:

```text
diff[1] = a[1]
diff[i] = a[i] - a[i-1]
a[i] = diff[1] + ... + diff[i]
```

For example:

```text
index       1   2   3   4   5
a          10  20  30  40  50
diff       10  10  10  10  10
```

The prefix sums of `diff` reconstruct `a`:

```text
10, 10+10, 10+10+10, ...  =  10, 20, 30, 40, 50
```

Now add `+7` to the range `[2,4]`. The desired new array is:

```text
index       1   2   3   4   5
new a      10  27  37  47  50
new diff   10  17  10  10   3
```

Only two differences changed:

```text
diff[2] += 7     # begin carrying +7 from position 2 onward
diff[5] -= 7     # stop carrying +7 after position 4
```

Why does this work? Every prefix sum before the left endpoint sees neither
change. A prefix sum from the left endpoint through the right endpoint sees
`+x` but not `-x`, so the value increases by `x`. A prefix sum after the right
endpoint sees both changes, whose total is zero. Thus a range update becomes
two point updates.

If a Fenwick tree stores `diff`, it can apply those two point updates in
`O(log n)`. The current value at position `i` is `prefix(i)`, also in
`O(log n)`. This is the range-add / point-query variant; it is different from
the earlier point-add / range-sum variant, where the Fenwick tree stores `a`
itself.

# Checklist

```text
Use 1-based indices internally.
Decide whether the tree stores values or differences.
For range sums, answer sum(r)-sum(l-1).
For inversions, count strictly greater values; duplicates are not inversions.
Use 64-bit integers for counts and sums.
```

# Minimal templates

C++:

```cpp
struct Fenwick {
    int n;
    vector<long long> bit;
    Fenwick(int n) : n(n), bit(n + 1, 0) {}
    void add(int i, long long delta) {
        for (; i <= n; i += i & -i) bit[i] += delta;
    }
    long long sum(int i) const {
        long long ans = 0;
        for (; i > 0; i -= i & -i) ans += bit[i];
        return ans;
    }
    long long range_sum(int l, int r) const {
        return sum(r) - sum(l - 1);
    }
};
```

Python:

```python
class Fenwick:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        self.bit = [0] * (n + 1)

    def add(self, i, delta):
        while i <= self.n:
            self.bit[i] += delta
            i += i & -i

    def sum(self, i):
        ans = 0
        while i > 0:
            ans += self.bit[i]
            i -= i & -i
        return ans
```

# Local exercises

- A. Point Add Range Sum: Maintain an array. Operation `1 i x` adds `x` to `a[i]`. Operation `2 l r` asks for the sum of `a[l..r]`.
- B. Inversion Count: Given an array, count pairs `i < j` with `a[i] > a[j]`. Values may repeat and may be large.
- C. Range Add Point Query: Maintain an array. Operation `1 l r x` adds `x` to every element in `[l,r]`. Operation `2 i` asks for the current value of `a[i]`.
- D. Offline Distinct Range Queries: For each static range `[l,r]`, count its distinct values. The queries may be reordered; attempt this blind before reading the editorial.

# Exercises

Use A for point-add/range-sum indexing, B to count inversions after coordinate
compression, and C to turn range additions into a difference Fenwick tree.
Use D as the blind synthesis problem: decide what each active Fenwick position
must mean while sweeping offline queries. Test index 1, the final index,
duplicate values, and queries supplied in an inconvenient order.

# Contest decisions, invariants, and traces

Do not choose a Fenwick tree because a problem says "array." Choose it when the
operations are additions and prefix aggregates, and both updates and queries
must be fast. A plain prefix-sum array makes queries `O(1)` but a point update
`O(n)`; direct summation makes an update `O(1)` but each range query `O(n)`.
A Fenwick tree gives both in `O(log n)`.

The invariant is precise: after any sequence of `add` calls, `bit[i]` equals
the sum of the original logical values in `[i-lowbit(i)+1,i]`. Prefix query
visits disjoint blocks that partition `[1,i]`; update visits exactly the block
owners whose block contains the changed position. These are the two facts to
prove before trusting the loops.

## Trace: point add and range sum

Start with `a=[2,1,4,3,5]`. Build by calling `add(i,a[i])`. For `add(3,+6)`,
the logical array becomes `[2,1,10,3,5]`; the visited owners are `3,4,8,...`.
For query `[2,4]`, compute `prefix(4)-prefix(1)=(2+1+10+3)-2=14`. Never try
to make `bit[3]` mean "the value at index 3"; it is a block sum.

## Trace: inversions with duplicates

For `[3,1,2,2]`, compress to ranks `[3,1,2,2]`. Read left to right. At the
third item, `seen=2` and `prefix(rank 2)=1`, so exactly one prior value is
greater. At the final `2`, the prefix count is two, so again one value is
greater. Equal values are included in the prefix and are therefore not counted
as inversions. The final answer is three.

## Difference trace

For `a=[10,20,30,40]`, store differences `[10,10,10,10]`. Adding `+5` on
`[2,3]` changes only `diff[2] += 5` and `diff[4] -= 5`, giving
`[10,15,10,5]`. Its prefix sums reconstruct `[10,25,35,40]`. This is why a
single Fenwick over differences solves range-add/point-query.

# Language notes and proof habits

Use 1-based internal indices: `lowbit(0)=0`, so an update starting at zero
loops forever. In C++, use `long long` for sums and inversion counts. In Python,
the integer size is safe, but buffered input and collecting answers before one
final print matter for large operation counts. Coordinate compression must use
`sorted(set(a))`, not `sorted(a)`, so equal values share a rank.

Before coding, say aloud which quantity `prefix(i)` represents. For normal
storage it is `a[1]+...+a[i]`; for difference storage it is the *current value*
at position `i`. This one sentence prevents most range/update mismatches.

| Wrong approach | Why it fails | Test |
|---|---|---|
| use index 0 | lowbit never advances | update/query at first position |
| use `seen-prefix(rank-1)` for inversions | counts equal values as greater | `[2,2]` |
| omit `r+1` subtraction | update leaks past the range | update `[2,3]`, query 4 |
| store sums in `int` | totals can exceed 32 bits | many large additions |

## Formative checks

1. Which blocks does `prefix(13)` read? Hint: repeatedly subtract lowbit.
   Answer: owners `13,12,8`, covering `[13,13]`, `[9,12]`, `[1,8]`.
2. Why is `previous - prefix(rank)` the inversion contribution? Answer: it
   removes every previous value `<=` the current value, leaving exactly `>`.
3. What two difference entries change for add `-7` on `[l,r]`? Answer:
   `diff[l]-=7`, `diff[r+1]+=7`.

# Submission workflow

Use a slow array model for stress tests: perform each update literally and
compute each query by a loop. Compare it with the Fenwick result on small random
arrays, especially negative additions, index one, index `n`, repeated values,
and a full-range update. Then run:

```bash
CP_TARGET=solution python3 sections/36_fenwick_trees/check.py
```
